::: {.lead}
The "Storm Night" package of lecture 27 is finished: a storyboard, a sound
set, a 30-second promo clip, a credits file and a check against the brief.
Today Salma, the producer, invites the teams to the review room of Night
Owl Games. Every team presents its package in **six minutes**. Then the
audience and the teacher give feedback, and each team turns the feedback
into a final version. Before you present, you review your own package with
**quality criteria** and **evidence**. Each section is one step of the
seminar and ends with a task. The team activity describes the whole
presentation, with an individual alternative for a student who works
alone.
:::

## Key terms

{{< glossary quality-criterion quality-review team-presentation constructive-feedback action-list final-delivery media-package production-log >}}

## 28.1 Step 1: review the package with quality criteria

Lecture 27 checked the package against the **brief**: lengths, formats and
peaks. A good package also needs **quality**: does it work for the players?
Five criteria answer this question (@fig-criteria).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 28.1 — Quality criteria and evidence"}
A **quality criterion** is one question that a reviewer asks about the
media. Each criterion needs **evidence**: something that the reviewer can
see, hear or measure.

- **Fits the gameplay:** does it show and sound like the level? Evidence:
  a gameplay shot next to the clip.
- **Consistent:** one art style and one sound mood? Evidence: panels, clip
  and sounds side by side.
- **Technical:** are the levels, the resolution and the length right?
  Evidence: the export settings and the peak meter.
- **Clear:** is the message clear in 30 s? Evidence: a viewer's
  one-sentence summary.
- **Rights cleared:** is every asset credited and allowed? Evidence: the
  credits file (lectures 25–26).

Each criterion gets a score from **1** (weak) to **4** (excellent), so the
package can score up to 20.
:::

![Five quality criteria with their evidence.](images/quality-criteria.png){#fig-criteria width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 28.1 — Team Blue's package"}
1. *Fits the gameplay:* the clip shows real gameplay of the rooftops in the
   rain, and the panels match the shots: **4**.
2. *Consistent:* the panels and the clip are dark blue, but the music loop
   is bright and happy, unlike the tense brief: **2**.
3. *Technical:* 30 s, 16:9, 1920 × 1080, peaks at −1.5 dB; one rain effect
   is quieter than the others: **3**.
4. *Clear:* a viewer says after one view, "Nour and Pasha escape a storm on
   the roofs": **4**.
5. *Rights cleared:* every asset has a TASL line, and the font licence is
   saved: **4**. Total: **17 of 20**.
:::

{{< sim file="sims/package-review.html" poster="sims/package-review.png" title="Package Review: score with evidence" height="820" >}}

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Scoring how much work the team did ("we worked all night, so it is a 4").
The audience only sees and hears the package. Score the evidence, not the
effort.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Review your package"}
In **Package Review**, score Team Blue's package and compare with the
teacher. Then score your own package on the five criteria, with one piece
of evidence for each score.

*Your result:* a review table with five scores and five pieces of evidence.
:::

## 28.2 Step 2: plan a six-minute talk

A **team presentation** shows the package and the work behind it. Six
minutes go fast, so the team plans every minute (@fig-talk).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 28.2 — The team talk"}
- **Order:** the brief and the package first, then the parts in the order
  of the handoffs (storyboard, sound set, promo clip), and the review last.
- **Roles:** in a team, every member presents the part of their own role.
- **Time:** six minutes in total. The promo clip (30 s) is **shown in
  full** and explained, so it needs at least one minute. The review, the
  credits and what the team learned need at least one minute too.
- **Show, don't read:** play the sounds, show the panels next to the shots,
  open the credits file. Slides carry pictures and a few words.
:::

![A six-minute team talk.](images/talk-plan.png){#fig-talk width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 28.2 — Team Blue's first plan"}
1. The first plan gives the producer 2 min for the brief, the artist 2 min,
   the sound designer 1.5 min and the editor 0.5 min.
2. The total is 6 min, but the promo clip cannot be shown in full in half a
   minute, and there is no time for the review.
3. New plan (@fig-talk): brief 1 min, storyboard 1 min, sound set 1 min,
   promo clip 2 min, review and credits 1 min.
:::

{{< sim file="sims/talk-planner.html" poster="sims/talk-planner.png" title="Package Talk Planner: six minutes" height="620" >}}

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Spending most of the time on the brief and the process, and then playing
the clip in a hurry at the end. The package is the star: show it in full.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Plan your talk"}
In **Package Talk Planner**, make a six-minute plan with the clip in full,
first for a team and then alone. Write the plan of your own talk: minute,
who, what.

*Your result:* a talk plan of six minutes.
:::

## 28.3 Step 3: present and give constructive feedback

After each talk, the audience gives feedback. Feedback only helps when the
team can act on it (@fig-feedback).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 28.3 — Constructive feedback"}
**Constructive feedback** has three parts:

- **What works:** a strength, named exactly ("the thunder hits on the cut
  at 0:12");
- **What to improve:** one problem, linked to a criterion ("the music is
  louder than Nour's voice line");
- **How:** a concrete next step ("lower the music by 6 dB under the
  voice").

Feedback is about the **package**, not the person. "The sound is bad" or
"I don't like it" gives the team nothing to do.
:::

![Constructive feedback: what works, what to improve, how.](images/feedback.png){#fig-feedback width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 28.3 — Three comments on Team Red"}
1. "Too long." The team knows there is a problem, but not what to cut.
2. "Why didn't you read the brief?" This blames the people.
3. "The clip is 45 s; cut the 15 s intro and start on the lightning shot."
   This one is constructive: problem, place and fix.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Giving only praise ("Nice!", "Good job!") to be kind. Praise helps too, but
only when it says exactly what works, so that the team keeps it.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Write feedback"}
During the presentations, write one piece of feedback for every other team
(or for the example packages of the teacher): what works, what to improve,
how.

*Your result:* feedback notes with three parts each.
:::

## 28.4 Step 4: act on feedback and deliver

Feedback becomes a better package only through an **action list**
(@fig-actions).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 28.4 — Action list and final delivery"}
An **action list** has one row per change: the **change**, the **owner**
and the **priority**:

- **must:** breaks a criterion of the brief or the rights (fix before the
  delivery);
- **should:** improves the quality clearly;
- **could:** nice to have, if time is left.

After the fixes, check the package against the brief and the criteria
again. The **final delivery** is one folder with the last version, for
example `storm_package_v03`: the storyboard, the sound set, the promo clip,
the credits file, the review table and the production log.
:::

![The action list of Team Blue.](images/action-list.png){#fig-actions width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 28.4 — Team Blue after the feedback"}
1. *Must:* a darker, tense music loop; the music lowered under the voice
   line. Owner: the sound designer.
2. *Should:* raise the quiet rain effect. *Could:* a shorter title card.
3. Version v03 scores 4 on "consistent"; the team delivers the folder
   `storm_package_v03` and writes in the log: "v03 delivered; title card
   for later."
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Trying to fix every comment before the deadline. Fix the musts first,
check again, and deliver on time; the "could" items wait.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Your action list"}
Turn the feedback on your package into an action list with owner and
priority. Fix the musts, check again, and deliver the final folder.

*Your result:* an action list and the final delivery folder.
:::

## Team activity: presenting the Storm Night package

::: {.callout-note title="Team activity · Presenting the Storm Night package"}
**Team:** the same team of three or four students as in lecture 27.

**Roles:** producer (brief, review, credits), storyboard artist, sound
designer, video editor; each member presents the part of their own role.

**Product:** the media package of lecture 27, with a review table on the
five quality criteria (section 28.1).

**Presentation:** six minutes, following the talk plan of section 28.2,
with the promo clip shown in full. Then two minutes of feedback from the
audience.

**After the talk:** an action list (section 28.4) and the final delivery
folder, with a last line in the shared production log.

**Individual alternative.** A student who works alone presents the same
smaller package of lecture 27 in the same six minutes and takes every role
in turn, in the order of the handoffs. The production log guides the talk:
for each role, one decision and one problem that was solved. The student
receives feedback in the same way and makes the action list and the final
delivery alone. The same five criteria are used for teams and for students
who work alone.
:::

## Case study: Feedback Desk

After the presentations, six situations need feedback: music that covers a
voice line, a storyboard that matches the clip, a clip that is too long, a
font without a licence, a team that asks "was it good?", and a student who
worked alone. The Game challenge of the interactive lesson uses these
situations. In the mini-game below you choose the most constructive
feedback each time.

## Further reading

Chandler, *The Game Production Toolbox* (2020), the chapter on
communication and reviews. Reynolds, *Presentation Zen* (3rd ed., 2019),
the chapters on simplicity and on showing instead of reading.

## Exercises

1. What is a quality criterion? Give an example with its evidence.
2. Name the five quality criteria of this seminar.
3. Why should you score evidence and not effort?
4. A package scores 4, 2, 3, 4, 4. What is its total, and which criterion
   should the team improve first?
5. In which order are the parts of a team talk presented, and why?
6. Why does the promo clip need at least one minute in the talk?
7. Name the three parts of constructive feedback.
8. Rewrite "The sound is bad" as constructive feedback.
9. What is the difference between "must", "should" and "could" in an
   action list?
10. What does a student who works alone present, and how is the work
    judged?

## Answers to the exercises

::: {.answers}
1. One question that a reviewer asks about the media; for example "fits
   the gameplay", with a gameplay shot next to the clip as evidence.
2. Fits the gameplay, consistent, technical, clear, rights cleared.
3. The audience only sees and hears the package; evidence can be checked,
   effort cannot.
4. 17 of 20; "consistent" (score 2).
5. The brief and the package first, then storyboard, sound set and promo
   clip in the order of the handoffs, then the review; the audience follows
   the production.
6. The clip is 30 s long and must be shown in full and explained.
7. What works, what to improve, how.
8. For example: "The rain effect at 0:20 is quieter than the others; raise
   it by about 4 dB."
9. Must: breaks the brief or the rights, fix before delivery; should:
   clearly improves the quality; could: only if time is left.
10. The same smaller package of lecture 27 in six minutes, every role in
    turn, guided by the production log; with the same five criteria.
:::
